#5240. AI Bias In HR: Why Polished Work Gets Overrated And What to Do About It

In today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work. In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect?

Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice.

One candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor.

AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it.

Indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words.

But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper.

An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job?

I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone says they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate.

CoderPad offers an interview environment where candidates use AI on realistic tasks while interviewers watch how they prompt, evaluate and revise the output. That gives employers a practical way to observe a skill candidates will increasingly need on the job.

I’d give every finalist the same flawed acquisition memo, the same source documents and access to the same AI tools. Then I’d ask what they would verify before sending the memo to a client. One might catch the double-counted revenue. Another might go further and work out whether the corrected numbers change the price we should offer. The most revealing moment may come when the tool confidently insists its original calculation was right. What does the candidate do then?

Lattice lets managers use AI to draft reviews from goals, feedback and meeting notes. Synq, formerly Gloat, says its software can build and run a review cycle from a plain-English instruction. These tools make it easier to collect and summarize evidence. That makes the choice of what to collect more consequential.

The selling spread across Asia’s AI supply chain. SK Hynix fell 11%, Samsung Electronics 9.9%, Advantest 12.9% and Tokyo Electron 12.5%. The Nikkei 225 lost 2.8%.

It followed another rough night on Wall Street. On Tuesday, Nvidia fell 5.9%, AMD 8.9% and CoreWeave 11.9%. Anthropic, the newest AI stock, closed at $81.91, below its $83 IPO price.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Measured from each stock’s own record high, the damage is deeper. CoreWeave is down 77%, Oracle 67% and SK Hynix 65%. Samsung and Tokyo Electron have both halved.

Crypto has not escaped. Bitcoin has tracked AI stocks lower since October. That suggests the same investors are cutting risk across both markets.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

Nvidia trades around the clock on Hyperliquid as a perpetual futures contract, a futures contract with no expiry date. The AI bubble has not popped in one go. It is leaking, one sell-off at a time. For now, the levels to watch are SoftBank’s ¥2,652 low in Tokyo and Nvidia’s $144 support.

#5237. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) community members have launched a new block explorer for Shibarium, the layer-2 network of the SHIB ecosystem, and Shiba Inu lead Shytoshi Kusama has remained silent on X since May.

Shiba Inu community veteran Mazrael announced the new explorer, scan.shibfun.app, in an X post. "Shibarium has a new block explorer," he wrote. According to Mazrael, the explorer was "built by the community, powered by ShibWatch, dressed in the Eternity Hub look."

The launch comes as SHIB trades near its lowest levels in years. In November, the price of SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021, and on Nov. 22, the token traded at around $0.00000362, according to CoinMarketCap.

According to the post, users can type a .shib name in the search bar and land on the wallet linked to it, and the explorer also shows new Shiboshis from Shibarium every day. For developers, Mazrael listed contract verification, read and write functions for contracts, the activity of ERC-4337 smart wallets, and a free API, which he described as "Etherscan-style too." Method names are decoded as well, and in Mazrael's words, there are "no more mystery 0x codes." The explorer also has a DApps page with Shibarium games and apps, and a button that adds Shibarium to a wallet in one click.

The work on the explorer is not finished yet. "Live blocks are complete now, and older history indexing," Mazrael wrote. On Tuesday, the explorer itself showed that 3% of Shibarium blocks had been indexed, and a notice on the site said that some of the counts may be inaccurate. Mazrael added that the new explorer can be found on Shib.io under ShibWatch.

Shytoshi Kusama's last post or interaction on X dates back to May 13, 2026. In September, Kusama changed his X bio to "Polish" and his location to "Close," and he has not explained the meaning of either word. The official Shibarium account on X has not posted since July 13, 2026.

Still, Shibarium updates kept coming from community members. In October, Mazrael said that CreateX, a standard factory for deploying contracts at the same address on different chains, went live on Shibarium. According to Mazrael, all 12 Safe v1.4.1 contracts were deployed to their canonical addresses through the Safe Singleton Factory, and x402 went live too, so AI agents can now pay in SHIB, TREAT and wrapped BONE.

In September 2025, attackers exploited the Shibarium bridge and withdrew about $2.4 million worth of assets from it.

According to Shibariumscan, Shibarium processed 546 transactions in a single day in late November, and on Oct. 31, the daily number of transactions on the network was 6,370. Since its launch in August 2023, Shibarium has processed more than 1.5 billion transactions in total.

At the same time, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan.

#5234. Your AI Startup’s Exit Is Being Shaped By The Deals You Sign Today

Valuations for AI companies have soared, and the companies are moving faster than ever. In the financings our firm has worked on so far in 2026, AI companies raised at median pre-money valuations up to 2.5 times those of non-AI companies from seed through Series C.

Across the broader private market, Crunchbase’s Current Valuation Model estimates that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board are worth about $2 trillion more collectively than their last reported funding-round valuations.

When everything moves that fast, the terms of your financings and of your contracts for compute, data and distribution get set early and in a hurry. Some of those terms will later slow a sale, add cost and erode value. The key is making sure you take long enough to consider what a deal does to your exit before you sign.

Take license-and-hire deals, where a buyer licenses your technology and hires your team instead of acquiring the company. They’ve become more common in AI, and the National Venture Capital Association has responded by updating its model charter. In 2025, it added an optional investor approval right over these deals, and sign-off by the board, including the investors’ directors, was enough to satisfy it.

The November 2026 update requires a vote of the preferred stockholders instead. Investors are often reluctant to use an approval right to block a deal. But it puts them at the negotiating table when an offer arrives, with a voice in how the proceeds are split between retention packages for the team and the cap table.

The stakes are higher when an investor is also a strategic partner. Nvidia and its NVentures investment arm alone have invested in more than 260 startups since the beginning of 2024, including 121 this year alone, Crunchbase data shows.

Strategic capital often comes tied to compute, cloud or distribution agreements. Those agreements can carry exclusivity, change-of-control and right-of-first-negotiation terms, and a right of first negotiation can force you to put a competing bidder on ice while you talk to your strategic investor first.

Be realistic about your leverage. Terms from the hottest AI rounds get cited as “market,” but what you can get depends on how much investors want your deal. Spend your negotiating capital on the few provisions that will matter most in a sale instead of trying to optimize on marginal topics.

An AI company’s most valuable assets are often the hardest to diligence.

Start with data. A buyer will want to know where your training data came from and whether your contractual rights cover how you use it and how the buyer plans to use it. Publicly available data isn’t necessarily licensed data. And permission to use a customer’s data to serve that customer doesn’t always cover training models for everyone else. If you fine-tuned on customer data under contracts that limit its use to serving those customers, a buyer may not be able to fold your models into its own products. The buyer may ask for a special indemnity, a larger escrow or a lower purchase price.

Your code gets similar scrutiny. In our deals, investors, and especially acquirers, now ask how much of the codebase was written with AI tools and whether those tools pulled in copyleft or commercially licensed code. We tell clients to audit their code regularly and fix issues as they surface. It makes that diligence conversation far easier.

Compute and model-provider contracts raise a different problem: a buyer may inherit a commitment it doesn’t want. Minimum-spend commitments, reserved capacity and exclusivity terms generally stay with the company in a sale. A buyer with its own GPUs may have no use for three more years of your reserved capacity, and it will factor the remaining payments into its offer.

All of this is easier to fix at the negotiating table than in the middle of a buyer’s diligence.

• Map who decides on a sale. Know which board and investor approvals it would trigger, including any approval right over a license-and-hire deal.

• Track your data and code rights. Record data sources and use restrictions and audit AI-generated code periodically.

• Stress-test your infrastructure commitments. Run cloud, GPU and model-provider obligations against slower growth and a sale.

• Keep strategic rights narrow. Limit the scope, duration and triggers of any right of first offer or negotiation you give a strategic investor.

• Read commercial contracts with an exit in mind. Check the change-of-control and termination rights before you sign.

Few founders are thinking about a sale when they close a seed round or sign their first GPU contract. You don’t have to predict the exit. You do have to know what you’re giving up each time you sign, so the speed that got you funded doesn’t cost you flexibility when the right acquisition offer arrives.

Aaron Rubin is a partner in Gunderson Dettmer’s Strategic Transactions & Licensing group and a leader of the firm’s artificial intelligence practice. He advises AI companies on strategic partnerships, technology and data licensing, and the development, commercialization, and deployment of AI products and services. His practice spans complex commercial transactions, intellectual property and data rights, and the evolving legal and regulatory issues shaping the AI industry. He also advises leading investors in industry-defining AI financings, including investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks.

Greg Volkmar is head of Gunderson Dettmer’s New York corporate group and co-chairs the firm’s growth equity practice. For more than 20 years, Volkmar has focused on advising early- and late-stage technology and life science companies through financings, corporate governance, and securities law matters. He is also a trusted advisor to leading venture capital, private equity and crossover funds on their US and global investment activities, such as equity and debt financings, mergers and acquisitions, and secondary liquidity transactions, as well as fund formation needs.

#5233. The Art of The Terrible Startup Name

When thinking of startup names, the usual question is how one identifies a great one.

But perhaps equally crucial is the reverse consideration: What makes for a truly awful startup name?

It’s a somewhat subjective exercise. Nonetheless, branding experts and occasional writers on the subject can agree on a few basic parameters. These include hard-sounding names, brands with negative connotations, and a certain ubiquitous suffix that could soon sound irrelevant.

Below, we look at each of these categories in more detail

One branding principle is that startups should avoid names that are unpleasant to pronounce. This includes words that sound too harsh or guttural, or are awkward in the native languages of potential users.

Unfortunately, it’s a principle often ignored.

For Athol Foden of naming consultancy Brighter Naming, the most prominent unpleasant brand name of recent quarters is Grok, the chatbot of Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Foden hates it so much he devoted an entire essay to what’s wrong with it.

“I still want to throw up when you say that name… and it is even worse in foreign languages,” he said in an interview. In his essay he called the brand a cross between “a suppressed swear word and a throat condition your doctor would prescribe antibiotics for.”

It’s not an anti-Musk stance. Foden is a fan of the entrepreneur’s Starlink as a name choice for the global satellite Internet service. It’s memorable and evocative in a positive way.

For other examples, we didn’t want to pick on current startups for their naming choices. So we looked instead to archives of startups past for other cases of harsh naming choices that didn’t pan out or are no longer operating under that brand.

Our shortlist included Quibi, a heavily funded short video startup with famous founders and a famously short shelf life. Others that have either folded or no longer operate under the original brand include Doostang, Gtrot, and Xobni (inbox spelled backwards, but not terribly clear how to pronounce.)

Another naming tactic to avoid is selecting a brand that evokes negative imagery or connotations.

“We always say: This is something you should be proud to wear on a hoodie,” said Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. If not, then reconsider.

Following this notion, one recently funded company name that rubbed both Benedini and your author the wrong way is Warhound, a startup focused on breeding dogs for roles in the military, law enforcement and emergency response that recently raised $200 million.

Sure, it’s memorable. But it sets an awfully aggressive tone, especially for a pet-pampering culture in which other startups promote offerings like dog spas, canine couture, and custom meals. While there’s a role for well-treated service dogs, it’s preferably far from any battlefield.

Or, as Benedini put it, “I’d be embarrassed to have Warhound on my hoodie.”

For other examples of less-than-stellar naming picks, we looked through the archives of startups past. One dud was Flud, which combines awkward spelling and imagery of a natural disaster. Boo.com, a defunct fashion site that was the iconic flops of the dot-com era also comes to mind, evoking fright more than the desire to shop. Another popular but questionable pick is Fire (sometimes alternately spelled Fyre), the chosen name of at least a dozen entries in the Crunchbase dataset.

It may still be in vogue to give your company a one-word name followed by AI. But don’t try to get a branding consultant to sign off on it.

Both Foden and Benedini advise against adding AI to the company name for multiple reasons. One is that it will likely sound dated going forward. Another criticism is that since virtually every startup incorporates AI to some extent, adopting a name with “AI” isn’t particularly meaningful.

If one does insist on an AI name, the minimum next step is to make sure it still works with those two letters on the end. Lots of companies — including Amazon (formerly Amazon.com) and Apple (initially Apple Computer) — have altered their names to keep up with the times and done just fine.

Despite all the advice on how to avoid an awful name, a part of me can’t help hoping more startups will just ignore it all. Then we could live in a world where startups sought funding with names like “Gruesome Grok AI” or “Festering Boil Labs.”

That said, there’s a reason startup naming is a serious endeavor, and bad choices often have equally bad consequences.

#5232. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5231. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

Anthropic stock has just completed one of the most dramatic post-IPO shakeouts in recent market history, and that violent reset may be exactly what sets the stage for an extraordinary rally. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that what looks like a failed debut could instead launch a move that redefines the stock’s valuation before the calendar turns to 2027.

Anthropic (ANT) priced its IPO at $83 and began trading on November 19. Shares exploded higher on the open, hitting $111.50 and briefly touching $115.10 before closing the first day near $97. The euphoria faded quickly. Over the next three sessions, the stock sold off hard, closing on November 24 at $81.91, below the IPO price, after printing an intraday low of $75.61.

In less than a week, the stock went from a multi-trillion-dollar peak-valuation fantasy to trading below its offer price. That kind of rapid digestion of early gains often clears out weak hands and resets sentiment for the next leg.

The hypothetical landmark catalyst is this: In the final weeks of 2026, Anthropic unveils a breakthrough version of Claude that achieves a decisive, independently verified leap in both capability and reliable alignment.

The release is paired with the announcement of exclusive, multi-year enterprise and government contracts totaling tens of billions in committed spend, including a landmark partnership that positions Claude as the preferred frontier model for several major sovereign AI initiatives.

The combination of technical superiority and locked-in, high-value demand triggers a violent re-rating as investors conclude the company has pulled decisively ahead of competitors just as the market was questioning AI valuations.

#5229. Flop Labs Pushes Back Testnet Launch Amid Final Preparations

Flop Labs has announced a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

Possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any plans to move the testnet launch to another day.

Flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

#5228. Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

#5227. Trezor Tells Crypto Users Never to Enter Wallet Backups on Phones Amid Theft Probe

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency users following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website."

According to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

According to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

The device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

The user said $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

Another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim says they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

On November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is currently no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

Trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are currently no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

@OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official UPDATE: This device came directly from Trezor and shows no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

In a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the company and showed no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

This appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an important security warning: users should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

#5225. Solana Validators Can Now Stop Block Processing

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

In periods of competing blocks, Solana validators spend CPU and timing resources replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another competing block from the same slot has been finalized.

This PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done. It also decouples functionality and gives control to Votor in requesting slot cancellation without modifying BankForks.

Overall, this is a reasonable technical improvement and has a good engineering motivation. Further technical comments and review would be helpful to understand if there are potential race conditions or issues with reliability of replay and consensus. This could be split into two PRs to make it easier to test and review.

Make sure that the replay thread doesn't block on the scheduler finishing processing blocks.

Add slot cancellation, where Votor can tell replay which blocks to stop trying to process.

There was an earlier PR (PR #16454) which attempted to solve a similar problem, but that PR included some complexity around being able to pause and resume block processing.

This PR attempts to solve a similar problem in a simpler way by adding slot cancellation. It allows validators to stop replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another block from the same slot has been finalized.

This is an efficiency-focused change to validator software. It's not intended to have a particular effect on transaction throughput or SOL price. For Solana to continue to perform well, it's important not only to continue to increase TPS but also continue to find ways to make sure that validators aren't doing unnecessary work.

For everyday users, it's unlikely there would be noticeable effects from this change. Sending/receiving SOL, using a DEX, using DeFi more broadly, and using any other Solana-powered website/app should all continue to function as normal. It's possible that users could see some benefits from this change in the form of Solana being more performant in the face of heavy compute loads.

#5224. Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a new company with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

“When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”

Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

“Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan said. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

“It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”

#5223. XRP News: Thanksgiving Rally or December 1 Supply Shock?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP has a history of making Thanksgiving interesting, old news for some. In 2024, Ripple surged nearly 49% in the three days following the holiday. Last year, it went nowhere. Now, XRP is heading into another Thanksgiving with $1 in sight and Ripple’s 1 billion-token escrow unlock looming on December 1.

The timing puts bulls in a tight spot. XRP is recovering from a November sell-off, but the rebound has yet to clear major resistance. A holiday rally could give buyers some breathing room before next week’s token release puts supply back in the spotlight.

The 2024 Thanksgiving weekend was anything but quiet for XRP. The token closed November 28 at $1.54, climbed to $1.80 the following day, and reached $2.29 by December 1. That was a gain of nearly 49% from Thanksgiving’s close.

The rally had fuel beyond holiday trading as Donald Trump’s election victory revived hopes for a friendlier crypto regulatory environment, while XRP was breaking out after years of being held back by its SEC lawsuit. Buyers were chasing momentum, and the long weekend did little to slow them down.

Last year’s price action was considerably less exciting. XRP closed Thanksgiving on November 27, 2025, near $2.20, then drifted around $2.16 over the following days. The market offered no repeat of the explosive move seen a year earlier.

That history makes this year’s comparison interesting, but the conditions are different. XRP is entering Thanksgiving after a painful November decline.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

XRP’s recovery toward $0.95 has brought the psychological $1 level back into play. Buyers have been defending the area below $0.90, preventing another immediate breakdown and giving the short-term chart some breathing room.

But the problem is overhead resistance, as XRP must first push through $0.96–$0.98 before $1 becomes a realistic breakout target. That zone has become the immediate test for buyers. A clean move through it could attract momentum traders and open the path toward $1.02 and $1.08.

The $1 mark matters because XRP has spent November losing ground. Reclaiming it would put the token back above an important psychological threshold and give bulls something concrete to work with.

Failure to break resistance could leave the rebound looking like another dead-cat bounce. XRP’s recent low around $0.89 remains the level to watch. Losing it would put $0.86 back on the radar and risk undoing the recovery.

For now, the chart is caught between an improving short-term bounce and a damaged larger trend. Bulls have a chance, but they need to turn that chance into a breakout.

The next complication arrives Monday, with Ripple’s scheduled escrow contracts. It will release 1 billion XRP, renewing concerns about supply just as the token tries to recover from bad geopolitical news.

The billion-token headline sounds worse than Ripple’s typical net release. Over the past year, the company has re-escrowed around 70% of monthly unlocks, leaving around 300 million XRP outside escrow on average. The market will be watching whether December follows the same pattern.

The full 1 billion XRP unlock is not equivalent to 1 billion tokens hitting exchanges for sale. What Ripple re-locks, retains, or moves afterward will determine how much circulating supply actually changes.

What does it need? XRP cannot afford to enter Monday with a failed breakout and weakening support. If buyers reclaim $1 before the unlock, sentiment could shift in their favor. If XRP remains pinned below resistance, the escrow event gives nervous traders another reason to stay cautious.

Thanksgiving delivered XRP a spectacular rally in 2024. This year, bulls need more than a holiday repeat; they need the $1 back.

#5222. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#5220. Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post.

Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

Traders on Polymarket now see about a 97% chance that the Fed raises rates at its December 8-9 meeting. That would be the Fed’s second hike of 2026, after September’s.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis report gave the Fed little reason to wait:

Strong incomes and sticky prices are the mix that worries a central bank. Polymarket’s December market puts a quarter-point hike at 94% and a half-point hike at 2.6%, with $58 million traded on it.

The year has turned around for the Fed. In January, two officials voted for a rate cut. By September, under Chair Kevin Warsh, who took over in May, the Fed raised its target range by 0.25 points to 3.75%-4%. In October, it held, but two officials wanted another hike. A hike sounds like bad news for crypto. This year’s data tell a more mixed story. We measured bitcoin’s move in the week after each 2026 Fed rate decision, from the open on decision day to the close seven days later.

The pattern fits an old market saying: sell the rumor, buy the news. By the time the Fed acts, a hike is often already in the price. Seven meetings and one hike is a small sample, so treat it as a clue, not a rule.

#5217. Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”

Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”

#5216. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

In its notice, Binance said that withdrawal services will be resumed when the network is deemed to be stable and that no further announcement may be made.

Those looking to transfer funds should make their withdrawals before the wallet maintenance is set to begin to avoid delays and possible loss of funds.

Wallet maintenance refers to a standard operational process that supports blockchain updates, system improvements, and fund security.

This comes weeks after Binance suffered an historic hack with $6.3 billion in assets affected. Binance has since completed coverage of assets impacted in the security incident and published a new Proof of Reserves snapshot.

In a recent development, Binance stated it has engaged leading security firms Mandiant, SlowMist and Verichains for independent reviews of its security procedures.

These reviews, the exchange said, will validate its current security infrastructure, assess its security posture going forward, and help strengthen the protections expected from the crypto platform.

Binance also stated that it was coordinating closely with the U.S. Department of Justice, as well as with industry partners who have assisted in freezing assets impacted by the security incident in late October 2026.  The collaboration is necessary throughout the asset forfeiture process, with the goal of supporting the return of affected funds as efficiently as possible.

In separate news, Binance said it has integrated the Cboe Global Indices Feed into its platform, app and Binance AI, giving users access to real-time traditional market data. The initial rollout covers three of the world's most widely followed U.S. equity benchmarks, with more benchmark data to follow: S&P 500 Index, Dow Jones Industrial Average, Nasdaq-100.

#5214. Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt

Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.

The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.

But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.

Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.”  Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.

It’s also become a big financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.

The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”

But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.

Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.

“We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.
